Senses.Note: The wedge is what blocks sight. Neishao says that seeing his staff, failing to see it, or simply setting it aside can all be caught up in the wedge; the work is to pull it out. Xiangya links that removal with opening the nondual gate, and Hengxiulin gives it as the third decisive turn. Huiyue pairs it with pulling a nail from behind the head. Yushan answers a monk who asks about passing the Buddha hall’s examination with the same phrase. Each use presses past a view that has become an obstacle.

Senses.Explanation: A comic epithet for a one-sided person: a fellow carrying a board and seeing only one side. The stock line says that Xu Six carries a board and sees only one side, while Baiyu Jingsi states directly that each party sees one side and is precisely a board-carrying fellow (各見一邊，正是擔板漢). In a case Baiyu raises, Muezhou Daozong calls to an addressee and applies the name when the man turns; Xuedou Chongxian and Huanglong Huinan then debate its application, and Baiyu judges their opposed comments one-sided. The label extends beyond that case. Dongshan Meixi Du says that learning without awakening is overbearing pride, whereas awakening without learning is a board-carrying fellow (有學無悟謂之增上慢，有悟無學謂之擔板漢). Zhe'an Jingfan applies it both to delight at a rich feast and fear in a thorn thicket, and elsewhere says that enumerating ranks, mysteries, divisions, reality, and expedients only makes such a fellow before asking how the matter can be raised whole (只成擔板漢。此事如何舉得全？). Yuanwu Keqin says that a board-carrying fellow often dies in the phrase (若是擔板漢。多向句中死却。). Zen bends a comic physical image into a public epithet for the person whom a record presents as fixed on one side or trapped in wording; the entry reports those attested applications without generalizing beyond them.

Senses.Note: Xuefeng says he has already met the assembly at Wangzhou Pavilion, Wushi Ridge, and before the monks’ hall. Two elders challenge where such meeting took place. Xuedou appraises their responses and closes, “Board-carrying Chan monks are as numerous as hemp and grain,” an image of people who see only one side of what they carry. Lingshu Yuan recites the case and writes a verse about meeting across the whole realm. Yuanwu tests Xuedou’s handling of Xuefeng’s invitation. Gulin asks his assembly whether anyone knows the place of meeting; Liao’an asks what place could be excluded from it. Their new turns keep the rebuke aimed at restricted seeing, not at a fixed geographical answer.

Senses.Explanation: To assume and bear responsibility, especially for the teaching or its succession. Yuanwu Keqin places successful shouldering beside accepting, heading toward, and carrying out; elsewhere he says only Shenguang was permitted to bear the subtle key of Shaolin. Guangzhi Quanwu calls for someone able to shoulder it with the whole body, and Xueqiao Yuanxin calls a person with strength to come forward and bear it on one shoulder. These responsibility, authority, and succession frames make the omitted load institutional and figurative. They are a different referent from physically carrying cargo, even though the metaphor retains the bodily image.

SearchAliases: carry snow to fill a well
Senses.Explanation: Carrying snow to fill a well is a recurrent comparison for ineffective effort, applied to talk, question-and-answer, sitting Chan, and other undertakings. Literally, "carry snow to fill a well" : the load melts while the well remains unfilled. Chan records use the concrete impossibility as a compact appraisal of ineffective religious display and effort. Baishan applies it separately to "pick it up and immediately use it", to question-and-answer exchanges in an enumeration beside "talking mysteries, drawing a cake to satisfy hunger", and to trying to pass through by silent stillness, contrasted with trying to state it in words as "proving a turtle to be a soft-shelled turtle". Tian'an calls sitting Chan like carrying snow to fill a well and rhymingly calls composing poetry kneading snow into a ball. Yinyuan pairs the phrase with trying to fill a net by blowing and says that even ages of such actions have no place. The Zen-specific use is a verdict applied not to an ordinary futile chore but to recognizable Chan-scene responses—silence, words, questions and answers, sitting, gestures, and other attempted displays.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Aim for a qilin, and you may not meet even a hare
SearchAliases: aim for a qilin, and you may not meet even a hare
Senses.Note: The saying warns that one may aim at a fabulous qilin and fail to meet even a hare. Yikui uses it after asking who can truly laugh at his words; Huitang answers a monk's comparison with it. Po'an says it in the abbot's room, and Huanxi uses it after a staff challenge. Xisou sets up an archer's shot and closes with the line; Chushi asks whether anyone will step forward before giving it. Each scene checks an ambitious aim against what can actually be met.

Senses.Explanation: To return to the root and source. The expression can name a turn toward original ground or the ninth stage of the oxherding sequence; Chan speakers also use it to ask whether seeking that return misses what is already present. Hansong Zhicao pairs a return to root and source with entering the marketplace, then asks who can perform the turn. Yushan Shangsi says that anyone wanting to return never leaves this one move and raises his whisk. Chushi Fanqi invites listeners to hear the sounds around them as a gate for returning, then says there remains a further turn. Buhui Fatong says old masters' myriad answers aim at release from birth and death and this one return before the eyes. Linquan Conglun, commenting on earlier teaching, says the route from beginning to end returns to the root and source without waiting through vast ages. Pu'an Yinsu warns his listeners not to mistake a building project for returning to the source; he asks them to understand mind and teaching. In a verse on an old case, Ruibai Mingxue pairs the image with a nose raised to the sky, opposing a futile chase after sounds and sights.

Senses.Explanation: This is what something is in itself, especially when the records set it against what that thing does. In the Blue Cliff Record, the source-unnamed questioner asks Zhimen Guangzuo what the perfection of wisdom is in itself, and Zhimen answers, ‘a bivalve holds the bright moon’; the paired question about its function receives ‘a rabbit carries young.’ Huanglong Huinan reworks the pair as ‘a pile of shit’ and ‘worms in the pile.’ Sixin Wuxin gives the same counter-answer, Ying'an Tanhua answers with meeting without courtesy, and Eryin Mi answers with flowers opening and spring birds singing. Elsewhere Yunfeng answers with an arrow piercing a willow leaf, Fayun Datong Shanben says ‘join,’ Qixin Haiyin sends the assembly to the hall, Foyuan Chegang points to the waves raised as soon as the tongue moves, and Muchen Daomin offers a starless steelyard with iron at both ends. Thus the word names the constituting side of the distinction, but the masters repeatedly make that apparent request for an abstract essence answerable by a concrete scene, encounter, or directive.

Senses.Explanation: The body exposed in the golden wind is Yunmen Wenyan's compact answer to the public question, 'When the trees are bare and the leaves have fallen, what then?' Later masters repeatedly raise, criticize, and answer the case, while verse authors carry its autumn scene into frost, leaves, river, moon and wind. 'Golden wind' is thus the autumn wind in the phrase's observable scene; the Chan pressure lies in presenting total exposure as the immediate answer, without supplying an object hidden behind it.
